newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels release two hostages, still defiant.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels release two hostages, still defiant.

text.p: Marxist rebels freed two more hostages -- leaving 81 inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima -- but their show of defiance crushed hopes the two- week-old crisis could end before the start of the New Year.

Dressed in suits and carrying plastic bags with personal belongings, Honduran ambassador Jose Eduardo Martell Mejia and Argentine consul general Juan Ibanez appeared in good health as they walked out of the residence late on Tuesday afternoon.
Ibanez, looking immaculate and still wearing a necktie, hugged Red Cross officials before the two men were driven away in a police car.
Argentina's Foreign Minister Guido di Tella expressed "the satisfaction of the whole Argentine government," at the release of Ibanez.
The remaining hostages included the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, dozens of Japanese businessmen and top Peruvian government and military officials.
The releases followed a carefully staged propaganda coup by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
The rebels invited journalists camped in the streets outside to view conditions inside the residence and to hear a series of militant messages.

MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini -- dressed in green military fatigues and covering his face with a red-and-white handkerchief -- said they would not drop their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
"We are inflexible in our original position," Cerpa said. "I do not see an immediate solution," he added, insisting the rebels were in "no hurry" to end the standoff.
The MRTA head said, however, that the group was "open to any mediator ... (Cuban leader Fidel) Castro or (Russian President) Boris Yeltsin or whoever."

The rebels paraded their key hostage, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, in front of reporters. A relaxed- looking Tudela said he spent his time in captivity thinking about the work piling up on his office desk and reading novels.
Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail party stormed two weeks ago by the rebels, was also brought before the cameras.
Looking grave and tired he apologised for the embassy's involvement in the crisis. "A thousand apologies from my government," he said in faltering Spanish.

In a brief walkie-talkie interview with Reuters, Cerpa said the MRTA had already achieved its aim of drawing world attention to the bad conditions of Peruvian jails, and would now concentrate on securing the release of prisoners.
He said responsibility for resolving the crisis lay with the government. "The government must reflect," Cerpa said.

He and about four younger rebels wearing combat gear and with ammunition strapped to their bodies met the group of about a dozen cameramen and photographers allowed inside the building for the first time since the crisis began.
Reuters photographer Zoraida Diaz, among the group, said Cerpa spoke calmly, insisting they were not terrorists and repeating demands for improved jail conditions for comrades.

Diaz said furniture was pushed up against windows inside the building as a barricade. "All the curtains were drawn and it was gloomy even though the lights were on... It was stuffy and sweaty but not unbearable. It smelt like a house that had been closed up for a long time," she said.
The rebels, who have booby-trapped and mined the property against posible attack, showed off their weapons including one grenade launcher.

Tuesday's burst of activity followed public expressions of hope from both Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and his Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi that the crisis would be brought to a peaceful end.
But their optimism was quickly undermined by Cerpa's comments and an earlier statement shouted by an unidentified rebel to reporters who approached the building.
The rebel slammed Fujimori's government as a "dictatorship dressed up as a democracy" that practiced "state terrorism that kills through starvation."

He said the guerrillas were "determined to make the ultimate sacrifice" in the siege. "Any harm to them (the hostages) will be the exclusive responsibility of the government of Mr. Fujimori if he decides upon a military intervention."
Amid tight security, Fujimori and members of his cabinet attended a Mass in the capital Tuesday held in honour of the 81 remaining hostages.

The rebels' defiant tone contrasted with a more conciliatory statement issued at the weekend after a first face-to-face meeting between the guerrillas and government negotiator Education Minister Domingo Palermo.

In an interview with the Spanish news agency Efe made available to Reuters, Fujimori said the crisis could be resolved without violence but insisted the guerrillas lay down their arms and free all the captives.
"I believe that in the end reason will impose a solution without the spilling of blood," he said.

Fujimori said he would not free any MRTA members from Peru's prisons. He said that if his government was to rule out the use of force, the rebels must put down their weapons and free the hostages to a "commission of guarantors."

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was confident of the Peruvian government's ability to handle the crisis -- so much so that he was going ahead with a five- nation Asian trip next week that officials had earlier said might be cancelled.
